q: What is Figure B that is a bracket used to hold and secure glass panels in place, often seen in glass railings and balustrades without full framing?
n: A glass clamp is a small metal bracket that grips the glass edge and fixes it to a post or wall, so railing panels can be held without full framing. Source: Glass hardware manufacturer literature (Dorma, Häfele); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure C that is a large exterior building system consisting of glass panels supported by a metal framework, creating a transparent facade?
n: A glass curtain wall is a non-loadbearing exterior wall of glass panels on an aluminum or steel frame, hung from the building structure and forming the facade. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; AAMA curtain wall manual.

q: What is Figure D that is a fitting with multiple arms used to connect and support glass panels at point-fixings in frameless facade systems?
n: A spider fitting is a cast stainless bracket with two to four arms. It holds glass panels at bolted points in frameless (point-supported) facades. Source: Glass facade manufacturer literature; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure E that is a type of post support used to hold glass panels vertically in frameless glass balustrades or pool fencing?
n: A spigot is a short stainless post fixed to the floor that clamps a frameless glass balustrade or pool-fence panel upright. Source: Glass balustrade manufacturer literature.

q: Which hardware can be specified for an entrance canopy?
n: Figure A, the point-fixed spider fitting, can support glass hanging overhead and is used for glass entrance canopies with laminated glass. Source: Glass facade and canopy manufacturer literature.

q: Which hardware is structurally appropriate for laminated glass?
n: Figure A, the point-fixed spider fitting, is used with laminated (typically tempered-laminated) glass, which stays in place if a pane breaks, as overhead and structural glazing requires. Source: Glass facade manufacturer literature; ASTM E2751 (laminated glass in structural applications).

q: Which hardware can be specified for tempered glass?
n: All the fittings shown (spider, clamp, patch, spigot) are made for tempered glass, which is strong enough to be drilled or clamped at points. Source: Glass hardware manufacturer literature; ASTM C1048 (heat-treated glass).

q: Which hardware can be specified for annealed glass?
n: Annealed glass is too weak at drilled holes and clamped edges and breaks into dangerous shards, so none of these frameless fittings may be used with it. They require tempered or laminated glass. Source: ASTM C1048; glass hardware manufacturer literature.

q: Which hardware can be specified for a large glass wall?
n: Large glass walls use Figure A, point-fixed spider fittings, which tie the glass back to a frame or fin so very large panes can be hung without mullions. Source: Glass facade manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used as a fitting for securing glass balustrades that include a continuous handrail for added safety and support?
n: Figure D, the slotted top rail (handrail cap), runs continuously along the top edge of the glass. It ties the panels together and gives a safe gripping rail. Source: Glass balustrade manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used for installing lightweight glass panels in display cabinets, providing secure but minimal fittings?
n: Figure C, small glass clamps, fix light glass shelves and panels in display cabinets with minimal visible hardware. Source: Glass hardware manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used in shower enclosures with sliding glass panels and providing smooth movement?
n: Figure B shows the roller and track connectors of a sliding shower panel, which let the glass glide smoothly. Source: Shower enclosure hardware manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used for mounting frameless glass balustrades, providing structural support without a handrail?
n: Figure E, a floor-mounted spigot, holds frameless balustrade glass upright with no top handrail. Source: Glass balustrade manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used in swing doors where glass panels are joined edge-to-edge, allowing a seamless look?
n: Figure A is the glass-to-glass hinge, which joins two tempered panels edge to edge, so a swing door hangs from a fixed glass side panel with a seamless look. Source: Glass door hardware manufacturer literature.

q: What glass has a metallic coating to reflect heat?
n: Reflective glass carries a thin metallic or metal-oxide coating that reflects a large share of solar heat and light, giving a mirror-like look from outside. Source: ASTM C1376 (coated glass); glass manufacturer literature.

q: What is a hollow, translucent glass unit made by fusing two halves with a partial vacuum inside?
n: A glass block is a hollow unit made of two pressed glass halves fused together while hot. As the air inside cools it forms a partial vacuum, making the block translucent and insulating. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Pittsburgh Corning (glass block) literature.

q: Which glass has minimal distortion?
n: Float glass is made by floating molten glass on molten tin, giving a flat, parallel, practically distortion-free surface. Tempering can add slight roller wave. Source: ASTM C1036 (flat glass); Pilkington float process.

q: Which glass lets you see the people inside at night when the lights are on?
n: Reflective glass mirrors the brighter side. At night the lit interior is brighter than outside, so people inside become visible from the street. Source: Glass manufacturer literature on reflective glazing; ASTM C1376.

q: What type of glass is translucent during the day but acts like a mirror at night?
n: Reflective glass looks mirror-like from the brighter side and see-through from the darker side. In daytime you can see out but not in, and at night it reflects on the inside while the interior is visible from outside. Source: Glass manufacturer literature on reflective glazing.

q: What material is used for windows to block excessive sunlight?
n: Solar tint (solar control film or tinted glazing) reduces glare and blocks a large share of solar heat and UV while keeping the view. Source: ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals (fenestration); window film manufacturer data.

q: Heat-absorbing glass in blue-green or gray cuts solar heat because of its:
n: Heat-absorbing (body-tinted) glass gets its color from metal oxides such as iron or cobalt added to the batch. This chemical composition absorbs solar radiation. Source: ASTM C1036 (tinted flat glass); glass manufacturer literature.

q: What gives double (insulating) glazing its thermal performance?
n: Insulating glass units trap a sealed layer of dry air or gas between panes. The gap sharply reduces conductive heat flow. Source: ASTM E2190 (insulating glass units); ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals.

q: What does fire-resistive glass contain between its panels?
n: Gel-filled fire-resistive glass contains a water-based clear gel between panes. In a fire the water absorbs heat as it evaporates and the gel turns opaque and insulating. Source: NFPA 80 / UL 9 (fire-rated glazing); fire glass manufacturer literature.

q: Which material is NOT advisable to use on the south side for energy conservation?
o: Heavy tinted glass and thick concrete wall
Transparent glass and light metal panels
n: At Philippine latitudes the sun tracks south of overhead much of the year, so south walls get strong sun. Clear glass and thin metal panels let in the most heat and are not advisable there. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015), building envelope; Olgyay, Design with Climate.

q: What is the standard face size of a glass block?
n: The standard glass block face is nominally 8 × 8 in. (about 200 × 200 mm), with 6 × 6 in. and 12 × 12 in. as other sizes. Source: Pittsburgh Corning glass block product data.

q: What is the main purpose of glass blocks?
o: Admitting light while obscuring the view
n: Glass blocks admit daylight while obscuring the view, giving privacy along with light. They are not stronger or cheaper than CHB. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Why do glass blocks insulate fairly well?
n: The sealed hollow, partially evacuated core of a glass block slows conductive heat flow, so its insulation is much better than single glazing. Source: Pittsburgh Corning glass block product data.

q: Where should glass blocks NOT be used?
n: Glass block is non-loadbearing infill, so it must never be used as structural members such as beams or columns, nor as furniture. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; manufacturer installation guidelines.

q: How are glass blocks installed?
o: Bedded in Portland cement mortar with steel rods in the joints, then sealed with clear silicone
Glued into a wooden frame with contact cement
Stacked like CHB with bars through the blocks
Stuck to concrete with grout and tile adhesive
n: Glass blocks are laid in portland cement mortar with horizontal steel joint reinforcement, then pointed and sealed with clear silicone. Bars are never threaded through the blocks. Source: Pittsburgh Corning installation guide; ACI 530 (masonry).

q: Where is wired glass best used?
n: Wired glass has a wire mesh embedded that holds the broken pieces together, so it has traditionally been used overhead in skylights and in fire-rated openings. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NFPA 80.
